paragraphs: Democrats won a wave of state and congressional races on Tuesday, including in Texas, and some of the winners had voiced opposition to the data center industry, according to Wired. Some in the tech world responded online by promoting data centers in orbit. Elon Musk posted on X early Wednesday that "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."

Wired reports that some companies are already trying to put computing in orbit. Google launched a satellite it says contains "data center class TPU," SpaceX says it aims to deploy "thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027," and Blue Origin has asked the FCC for a permit to launch 50,000 satellites. Wired adds that space-based data centers are much more expensive than land-based ones, cannot grow to hyperscale size and depend on the risks of satellite launches.

TechCrunch says the results gave Democrats full control of Congress. It cites an NBC exit poll in which almost 80% of respondents opposed data centers in their neighborhoods and almost 60% called them a crucial or major factor in their vote. It names Texas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina as states where winning candidates opposed rapid buildout. Likely next steps, it says, include construction moratoriums and rules making data centers pay for their own grid upgrades. Goldman Sachs predicts construction delays in Georgia and Texas.

There are limits. Wired's experts note that Republicans still control the Texas Senate, and developers there hold strong vested rights, while counties have limited zoning power. TechCrunch says a national moratorium bill from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez would face a possible veto, and that even some Democrats contest a blanket freeze. Public Citizen's Adrian Shelley told Wired the industry has shown little interest in working with lawmakers. The industry's own response was not reported in either piece.

NASA unveiled a new experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, on Wednesday at the UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The agency describes it as a high-performance, highly adaptable research platform designed to speed the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.

According to NASA, the X-70 is crewed and uses advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will let the agency explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. It can carry up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations. NASA lists a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds, a cruise speed of Mach .75, a ceiling of 45,000 feet and a range of more than about 1,726 miles.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the plane's modular design and ability to swap payloads quickly will keep teams flying and learning. He said NASA expects the aircraft's first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years. Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division in NASA's Research and Technology Mission Directorate, said it was exciting to add another X-plane to drive aeronautics research.

NASA placed the X-70 in a lineage that includes the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and the current X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator. The agency says the new aircraft will expand its capacity for experimental flight research. The first flight, which NASA puts within two years, is the next milestone to watch.

Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study reported by The Guardian. The research was led by Cefas, a British government agency, and published in Science Advances.

The team projected climate impacts on four key groups of marine life under a scenario of 3C of warming by 2100. They found fish and seabed invertebrates may become more diverse by mid-century, by about 12%, while phytoplankton and zooplankton diversity could fall by about 3% and 7% by 2050. Cefas ecologist Elena Couce, a co-lead author, said the results challenge the expectation that biodiversity would rise across the board in middle latitudes such as the UK.

Co-lead author Lily Greig said that if predator diversity rises while prey diversity falls, the food chain could be disrupted, and that gains in some groups do not necessarily mean the ecosystem is becoming more resilient. The seas around the British Isles, particularly the southern North Sea, have been identified as marine climate hotspots, among 20 worldwide that have warmed fastest over 50 years.

The researchers say the work could serve as an early warning system showing where biodiversity is changing fastest. It has been submitted to the government's review of marine protected areas, which is looking at fishery management measures. Couce said policymakers need to account for climate-driven biodiversity change before making other management plans. The study used long-term datasets and machine-learning techniques to project change to 2100.

An archaeologist argues that Verica, the Iron Age British ruler who persuaded Emperor Claudius to invade in AD 43, was probably a woman rather than the king historians have assumed. Miles Russell of Bournemouth University sets out the case in his forthcoming book on Caratacus and in a Current Archaeology article, according to New Scientist and The Guardian. The Guardian calls the theory controversial.

Russell points to several lines of evidence. Iron Age British names ending in "a" are usually female, he says, in about 95 per cent of cases. Coins bearing Verica's name tend to show female warriors on horseback. He says the inscription read as "son of Commios" could equally mean "daughter of," and that "rex" was not gender-specific.

Other experts are split. Katharina Rebay-Salisbury of the University of Vienna called the argument highly compelling but was sceptical of the coin imagery, since the figures are stylised. Roger Tomlin of Oxford said the masculine form "Vericus" is the best argument that "Verica" was feminine, but that there is little evidence "rex" was used for female rulers and that Russell must find other examples. He also said the coin figure does not prove Verica's sex. Daphne Nash Briggs said some coins appear to show a clearly male rider or a head with an Adam's apple. Russell argues that image depicts the emperor.

Russell says he welcomes debate. He argues the idea fits Cassius Dio's portrayal of Claudius as influenced by women, and fits findings from his 2025 DNA study suggesting women held significant status in Iron Age southern Britain.

A UK law taking effect on November 6 will ban the possession or publication of pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation, and also content depicting simulated incest between people not related by blood, according to Wired. Content showing performers role-playing as minors under 16 is also covered. Offenders face up to five years in prison and a fine.

The amendments to the Crime and Policing Act stem from a pornography review by Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin. She cited anecdotal evidence that simulated incest content can be used by abusers to permit abuse of children. She told the BBC that porn has normalized sexual violence, and the strangulation measure followed concern over deaths linked to choking during sex.

Critics say the wording is too broad. Obscenity lawyer Myles Jackman told Wired it could capture harmless content such as breast smothering or even oral sex, and called it one of the greatest acts of suppression of free speech in global history, though he has no objection to the strangulation ban itself. Creator Alexandra Snow worried about how it will be interpreted and about automated image-recognition flagging. Many creators are reportedly removing clips. OnlyFans creator Cami Strella said a ban could push worse content underground.

The UK Ministry of Justice denied the law is meant to curb sexual expression. Spokesperson Clara Coleman said the goal is to halve violence against women and girls in a decade, and that the laws target content that normalizes violence. How the law is enforced is the next thing to watch.

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele posted videos on Wednesday of heavily armed Salvadoran soldiers patrolling streets in Haiti, according to Al Jazeera. "Gather your gangs so we can go fight with them," he wrote on X. Haitian authorities say they found the burned remains of a truck used by four Salvadoran aviation technicians attacked by gangs on October 18, but have not found the men.

The disappearance prompted Bukele to send more than 2,000 troops and military hardware. Police found the vehicle on Tuesday in the Santo neighbourhood outside Port-au-Prince during a joint operation with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force and Salvadoran troops. Bukele also posted a video he said showed Salvadoran helicopters firing on gangs attacking Chadian GSF soldiers.

The deployment has raised questions over who is responsible for the use of force. UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric said only about 200 of the Salvadoran soldiers fall under GSF jurisdiction, and that operations must respect international human rights law. Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime said foreign forces operate under Haitian authority and came to support the state. A gang leader, Wilson Joseph of the 400 Mawozo, told the Associated Press he had asked the UN Secretary-General for dialogue.

Doctors Without Borders said 30 people were injured in the eight days after October 18 and fears more victims and displacement with additional forces arriving. Haiti has had no elected government since 2021, and national elections have been delayed from December 13 to July 18, 2027. Some 5.94 million Haitians face acute hunger, according to an international assessment.

Bob Dylan met Pope Leo XIV at the Apostolic Palace in Rome on Wednesday, between concert dates in Italy, according to NPR and the BBC. The Vatican said the encounter was brief. Leo gave Dylan a rosary, and Dylan gave the pope a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One."

Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro of the Vatican culture ministry and Andrea Monda, editor of L'Osservatore Romano. Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with the pope and the two met privately for a few minutes. Dylan, who is 85, wore dark clothing and a hoodie. He played Milan on Monday and is due to play Rome's Palazzo dello Sport on Thursday on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.

The link between the two men has a literary side. Leo, who was born in Chicago, quoted Dylan's unreleased 1963 song "Go Away You Bomb" in the preface to his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift," warning against rearmament and nuclear weapons. The typewritten lyrics were never recorded and went unpublished until they were found and put up for auction in 2013, according to the BBC, citing the New York Times.

It was Dylan's second meeting with a pope. In 1997 he performed for John Paul II in Bologna, and John Paul quoted "Blowin' in the Wind" in his sermon. NPR notes Dylan won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.

A Brazilian under-20 match in Minas Gerais ended with a record 53 red cards after a mass brawl, according to Al Jazeera. The first leg of a state championship semifinal between Uberlandia and Mamore was played on Sunday. Referee Fernando Patrick Drosghic Modesto sent off 43 players, eight members of coaching staff and two Uberlandia board members.

In his report, the referee said trouble began early in the second half when several Uberlandia officials invaded the field after one of their players was sent off. The match was halted for 40 minutes and then restarted. Mamore scored in the ninth minute of stoppage time to lead 3-1. Brazilian media reports say Mamore player Davi taunted Uberlandia players during the goal celebrations, which set off the brawl.

The referee wrote that a generalised brawl made it impossible to show the red cards or carry out the match-closing protocol, so he declared the match over because of the turmoil and lack of security. He added that a police report was filed over threats against him, and that Mamore's team vandalised the dressing room afterward.

The previous Guinness World Record was 36 red cards, in a fifth-division match in Argentina in February 2011. On Wednesday, Uberlandia said it would forfeit the second leg as a gesture of fair play, because Mamore did not have enough eligible players. That sends Mamore to the tournament final. Uberlandia said it has taken internal disciplinary measures.

Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced on Thursday to 10 years in prison for conspiracy to collude with foreign forces under the national security law Beijing imposed in 2020, according to the BBC and NPR. Wong, who turned 30 last month, pleaded guilty in September. NPR reported that Judge William Tam considered a 13-year starting point but reduced it because of the plea, and rejected the idea that Wong's role was limited.

Wong is already serving a four-year, eight-month term in the city's biggest national security case, linked to an unofficial primary, and had been expected to be freed in January 2027. The judge said two months and two days of the new term will run concurrently with that sentence.

Prosecutors said Wong conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing. The BBC said the court heard the activities took place between July and late November 2020. NPR said prosecutors pointed to his meetings with US politicians including Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio.

Reactions differed. Chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability." Authorities say the law is needed to maintain stability. Human Rights Watch called the ruling "cruel and unjust," and fellow activist Frances Hui said she was "heartbroken" and "outraged." Eric Lai of the Georgetown Center for Asian Law said such charges can be "repeatedly weaponized" to keep a political prisoner in jail.

The BBC noted that the harshest sentence under the law so far is the 20 years given to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai. NPR reported that Wong's lawyer had asked for a sentence that would give his client some hope, saying Wong wants to care for his parents after release.

Hubert Aiwanger, deputy leader of the German state of Bavaria, was found dead in a Berlin hotel room on Wednesday, police said, according to The Guardian. He was 55. The cause of death was not immediately clear, and police and prosecutors have opened an investigation.

Their joint statement said the aim of the inquest is to establish the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, and to rule out any possible third-party culpability. They gave no further details. Police said he was found in the Berlin-Mitte district.
The Bild daily reported that Aiwanger was in Berlin for the opening of an office for his party but missed the event because he felt unwell. It said police later discovered his body in the hotel.

Bavarian state premier Markus Soeder called the death an "absolute tragedy." He said everyone was deeply shocked and that thoughts were first with Aiwanger's family and children. German media reported that Aiwanger had two children and lived with his partner.

Aiwanger led the populist Free Voters party and served as Bavarian economy minister. He had headed the party's Bavarian branch since 2006, and under him it entered the state government for the first time in 2018 as a junior partner to Soeder's Christian Social Union. It never won enough seats to qualify for the federal parliament.

In 2023 Aiwanger faced national controversy after reports that he wrote an antisemitic pamphlet as a 17-year-old schoolboy. He denied writing it but admitted having had "one or a few copies" in his school bag. He apologised and refused to step down.

South Korea plans to expand the operations of its anti-piracy Cheonghae unit to waters closer to the Strait of Hormuz, the defence ministry said, according to The Guardian. The move follows pressure from US President Donald Trump for Seoul to support his war in Iran. The government will submit a motion to parliament extending the unit's area to waters near the Omani port of Duqm, about 650km from the strait. President Lee Jae Myung and the cabinet must also approve it.

A defence ministry official said the aim is to protect citizens and economic interests. He said the reinforcement is strictly non-combat and the unit would operate independently of allied forces. Operations would stay in open waters south of Oman, and patrol aircraft would be barred from targeting or monitoring Iranian territory, territorial waters or the inside of the strait.

The motion would also extend the unit's Middle East deployment, which expires at the end of 2026. The unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009. Reports cited by The Guardian say it now includes a destroyer, a helicopter and about 300 personnel, and that Seoul would add a P-8A patrol aircraft and 75 more personnel.

Trump has criticised South Korea for what he called insufficient support and scaled back major joint military drills this summer. South Korea sourced 70 percent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025, mostly via Hormuz, the industry ministry said.

Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire after trying to use unauthorised routes through the strait. Lee said in September he would not deploy assets in a way that could draw the country into conflict.

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman oversaw the signing of several agreements on Wednesday, including a defence cooperation deal and more than $403 million in Saudi loans, Al Jazeera reported. It was al-Sharaa's second visit to Riyadh in under a month; the two last met on October 6.

Syria's Foreign Ministry called the defence agreement between the two defence ministries the most notable of the deals but did not disclose its terms. It came days after Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Syria was evaluating whether to join a mutual defence pact among Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, which he called the Mecca alliance.

The Saudi Press Agency said the Saudi Fund for Development agreed six concessional loans with Syria's Finance Ministry: $100 million for rebuilding healthcare facilities, $60 million for repairing housing, $105 million for civil defence, $90 million for the Aleppo thermal power plant and $30 million for drinking water in Damascus and Idlib. The governments also signed memoranda on industrial cooperation, agriculture and environmental protection.

According to the Syrian Foreign Ministry, the leaders discussed regional tensions, shipping safety and energy supplies. They urged an immediate end to actions threatening navigation in the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Strait of Hormuz.

Syrian researcher Ahmed Qassem told Al Jazeera the repeat visit shows the scale of security challenges, and argued Syria should join the alliance to deter Israeli encroachment. Saudi Arabia has backed Syria's government since al-Sharaa came to power after Bashar al-Assad was overthrown in December 2024.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog accepted the certified results of last week's election on Wednesday and began consulting party leaders on who should form the next government, Al Jazeera reported. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has made unsubstantiated claims that the vote was stolen. Israel's elections commission said its investigation found "no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results."

In the October 27 vote, neither Netanyahu's coalition, with 53 seats, nor opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc, with 48, reached the 61 needed. Arab-led parties Ra'am and the Joint List won a record 19 seats. Ra'am said it would recommend Eisenkot, bringing his expected support to 56, according to Ynet. Channel 12 reported the Joint List was expected to coordinate with him, which could push him past 61. Netanyahu's bloc may not produce 53 endorsements, since Degel HaTorah said it would back neither man.

Herzog will choose the candidate best placed to form a coalition, then the nominee has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. If neither succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year. Herzog urged both camps to compromise and condemned "racist expressions" aimed at Palestinian-Israeli voters.

Separately, opposition figures including Yair Lapid said Democratic gains in the US midterms show Israel cannot afford Netanyahu. Eisenkot pledged to restore bipartisan ties with Washington. Netanyahu did not immediately respond to that criticism, and his response to the commission's findings was not included in the reports.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Democratic gains in the US midterm elections could bring more help for Kyiv, Al Jazeera reported. Democrats won both the Senate and the House. In an interview with German broadcaster ZDF, Zelenskyy said Democrats speak clearly about supporting Ukraine and renewing the US-Europe connection, so there is hope more support will follow.

European reactions were mixed. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she hoped the new Congress would keep supporting Ukraine and put more pressure on Russia. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was sceptical that Trump would change course, noting that Trump has largely governed by bypassing Congress. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the result could create an opportunity for a fresh initiative to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Austria's foreign minister said European security must not depend on US voting.

In recent weeks, Al Jazeera noted, Trump has made moves favourable to Russia, including a deal to import Russian diesel and a waiver of sanctions that Congress had approved. Ukraine has also accused Washington of delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia hopes Trump will continue his peacemaking efforts regardless of the election result.

Democratic aides told US media that helping Kyiv would be a priority when the party takes control of the congressional agenda in January. Diplomacy is moving faster. Envoy Steve Witkoff said Washington would bring Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. Zelenskyy said he had detailed conversations with Witkoff and Jared Kushner beforehand and wrote that negotiations must move forward at full throttle.

Democrats will control both houses of Congress from January, and The Guardian and Al Jazeera both report they are likely to try to limit President Donald Trump's foreign and economic policies. Both note the limits of that power: Democrats cannot override a presidential veto on their own, and Trump has said he will "veto everything," according to Al Jazeera.

The Guardian says the likely leverage point is the budget. A government funding measure expires in the December lame-duck session, and Democrats could also press for concessions on Iran or limits on Trump's authority in the National Defense Authorization Act, which would authorise about $1.15 trillion for 2027. Former diplomat Ryan Crocker said the Pentagon's request for more Iran war funding would be the first battleground, but warned that shutting down the government could be a "two-edged sword."

The Guardian notes that in 2019 Congress passed a resolution to end US support for the Saudi war in Yemen, and Trump vetoed it. Carnegie scholar Jennifer Hendrixson White said it is unclear whether investigations into the Iran war or defence contracts would turn into meaningful action.

Al Jazeera adds that most bills need 60 Senate votes, but Democrats gain confirmation power and committee subpoena authority. Economist Dean Baker said they could attach healthcare measures to must-pass spending bills, making them harder to veto. Many Democrats plan to investigate the Trump family's wealth.

Republican reaction is also divided. The Guardian reports Vice President JD Vance said "the reason we lost is the war," while Trump said the war was worth it, adding that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said in a long post on X on Wednesday that Republicans suffered a "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections, according to Fox News. He called the result a "Watergate-level repudiation" and wrote that Republicans "lost every single statewide election" in Texas.

According to the Fox News Decision Desk, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race, the first Democratic Senate win in Texas in nearly four decades. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott. Fox also reported Democratic wins in the lieutenant governor and attorney general races.

Cruz tied the losses to the cost of living. "Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high," he wrote, adding that elected Republicans "didn't do enough to address their very real pain." He also criticized tariffs and the prolonged war with Iran, and said Republicans lost ground with blue-collar workers, young voters, farmers, ranchers and Hispanic voters. The Washington Examiner reported that he noted pre-election polls showing cost of living as the top voter concern and acknowledged the party did not focus enough on it. The Examiner described Cruz as a possible 2028 presidential candidate.

Cruz said he called Talarico to congratulate him and was willing to work with him on issues that benefit Texas. Fox reported that Paxton, President Donald Trump and other national Republicans had labeled Talarico a "communist" during the campaign, while Talarico described himself as a moderate. Cruz wrote that Texas had not become "a bunch of tofu-eating, gun-banning, tutu-wearing pinko commie liberals," and predicted, "Texas will be red again." The text did not include a response from Democrats to his remarks.

Five Republican candidates who had cast doubt on, or voted to block, Joe Biden's 2020 victory lost races for governor in major battleground states on Tuesday, according to Al Jazeera. They were Rep. Andy Biggs in Arizona, Rep. John James in Michigan, State Treasurer Stacy Garrity in Pennsylvania, Rep. Tom Tiffany in Wisconsin and billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia.

Al Jazeera reported that Biggs and Tiffany voted in January 2021 to overturn the 2020 results as House members, and both signed onto a lawsuit seeking to invalidate results in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Garrity appeared at a January 5, 2021 rally calling on Pennsylvania lawmakers to decertify the results. Jackson called Biden's win "totally ridiculous." James acknowledged Biden's win in 2022 but said in June that the 2020 election was "rigged and manipulated." Tiffany, Garrity and Jackson have since acknowledged that Biden won, the outlet said, while Biggs and James have not. Al Jazeera said it asked the offices of Biggs and James for comment and had not yet heard back.

The outlet noted that in some states governors play a major role in voting access, election administration and congressional redistricting, and that these battleground states will matter in the 2028 presidential race. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican, said Wednesday he would not call a special legislative session to redraw congressional maps before his Democratic successor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, takes office. Al Jazeera said it is unclear whether the redistricting push will keep its momentum. Trump told The New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the midterm results.

New Zealand votes on November 7, and polls show the governing centre-right National Party and the centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, according to Al Jazeera. Neither is on course to win enough seats to govern alone, so smaller parties could decide the outcome.

The country uses a mixed-member proportional system in which voters cast one ballot for a local candidate and one for a party. The party vote determines each party's overall share of the 120 seats, and a majority usually means 61. A party needs 5 percent of the party vote or one electorate win to enter parliament. Every government since 1996 has been a coalition led by Labour or National, except in 2020, when Labour governed alone.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is seeking a second term. He leads a coalition with New Zealand First and ACT, and Al Jazeera reported that he survived two attempted no-confidence votes by National MPs this year. Labour leader Chris Hipkins, a former prime minister, hopes to return to office. National is pledging a return to budget surplus and an expanded national pension scheme. Labour is focused on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.

The real contest, Al Jazeera said, is between two blocs. National would need both coalition partners again, while Labour would depend on the Greens and possibly Opportunity. If a small party misses the 5 percent threshold and wins no electorate, its votes produce no seats, which could cost its bloc a majority. Extra seats could also raise the bar: if parliament grows to 122 seats, a bloc would need 62. Polls suggest Te Pati Maori may again win more electorates than its vote share entitles it to.

The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the June 2016 Brexit referendum, according to the BBC. Sterling has gained notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected interest rate rise.

The BBC said the most-watched measure, which tracks sterling against a basket of 18 major currencies, reached a joint highest level this week, according to Bank of England figures. It stood at 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank is due to officially confirm the calculation on Thursday. As of 04:15 GMT on Thursday, the pound was up 0.13% against the dollar at $1.3495 and down 0.16% against the euro at 1.1979 euros.

Sterling fell significantly after the 2016 referendum and hit further lows during the Brexit process, the Covid pandemic and the 2022 mini-Budget. Some traders told the BBC the UK is now seen in a different light because of relative political stability, solid growth and a rapprochement with the European Union. Economist and former Treasury minister Jim O'Neill said he was not surprised, arguing that people were, and to a lesser extent still are, underestimating the improving momentum in the UK.

The BBC noted that a stronger pound can help rein in inflation and increase consumers' buying power on imports and holidays. UK growth this year has outperformed all forecasts, though there are signs that higher energy and fuel prices have hit consumer confidence. The Bank's nine-member Monetary Policy Committee decides on interest rates on Thursday, and the BBC said the first rise in three years is widely expected.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government tries to save the discount retailer from collapse, the BBC reported. Poundland is on the brink of insolvency, and its owner, Gordon Brothers, has rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk. The meeting was originally due on Thursday but was brought forward.

Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, said it is "pursuing all avenues through the sales process" and described the company as "challenged and vulnerable." It said Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level." A source close to Reynolds said Gordon Brothers committed in the meeting to prioritise bids that protect workers and stores, though it remains unclear whether the firm will keep the business together or break it up.

Poundland's managing director, Barry Williams, told the BBC the company is profitable and sales are growing. Founder Steve Smith said two offers are on the table and that a collapse could affect up to 30,000 people including suppliers. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged Gordon Brothers to "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores." Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said the committee has asked the owners to appear on November 11 to explain why they have not accepted what he called a fully funded deal.

Poundland has filed notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from creditors until next Thursday. The BBC said buyers are currently understood to be interested in only about half the stores, which would leave roughly 6,000 employees without jobs. Suppliers warned of losses; one said some smaller firms would not survive Poundland's collapse.

The UK is "dangerously" dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, according to a parliamentary investigation by the House of Commons business select committee, as reported by The Guardian.

The committee called for an urgent centralised policy and a "critical minerals finance facility" that would use grants, equity and debt to help fund rare earth and other mines and speed diversification. Committee chair Liam Byrne said Britain cannot rearm, build AI or deliver net zero without securing these minerals, and that 16 years after China first used its hold over rare earths as a weapon, Britain "remains dangerously exposed."

The committee found the main bottleneck is processing, where China dominates the refining of seven categories of minerals. MPs were told demand for lithium would rise 45-fold by 2030 and demand for rare earths used in permanent magnets would rise 16-fold. The report noted China cut off rare earth supplies in 2025. It said Donald Trump secured a reprieve on Chinese export restrictions, extended to January 2027, which leaves the UK at the mercy of US-China relations. The most realistic solution, the committee said, is working with G7, European and Indo-Pacific partners to aggregate demand and bring in new suppliers.

The committee also said government transparency was lacking and that it could not be confident the government could meet any of the 10 tests in its plan. A government spokesperson denied there was no critical minerals strategy, citing £400m to ramp up domestic production and recycling. The spokesperson said the strategy sets 2035 goals, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any mineral coming from one country.

Figma shares fell 7% in extended trading after the design software company reported third-quarter results and guidance that beat Wall Street expectations, CNBC reported. Revenue grew about 43% from a year earlier, and the net loss narrowed to $81.3 million, or 15 cents per share, from $1.10 billion a year earlier. Its 12% adjusted operating margin exceeded the 6.1% analysts expected, according to StreetAccount.

Executives raised the full-year forecast to $1.497 billion to $1.499 billion in revenue, up from $1.463 billion to $1.467 billion, and lifted the operating margin outlook to 11% from 9%. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected $1.471 billion. Figma sees fourth-quarter revenue growth slowing to about 33%, though analysts had predicted 28%.

The company said that during the quarter it began giving clients more AI credits while holding prices steady. Chief financial officer Praveer Melwani told CNBC this means "potentially trading off near-term revenue" to invest in customers and allow durable growth over the long term. Figma said weekly users of AI credits at organizations spending over $10,000 rose almost 50%, the share of work done by its own AI model doubled, and the rate of people undoing AI-generated work fell. Melwani said Figma is open to powering actions with its own model if it offers lower latency, lower cost or similar quality to third-party options.

CNBC said the shares are down about 41% this year while the S&P 500 has gained 12%, after earlier investor worries that AI models could threaten Figma's business. CEO Dylan Field said the company is increasing its focus on cybersecurity, noting that AI agents have infiltrated systems at Hugging Face and other companies. The announcement came a day after Canva said it would cut 22% of its employees.

A former Samsung Electronics employee who later joined Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, was reportedly sentenced by the Seoul High Court on Oct. 22 to five years in prison for leaking Samsung's technology, CNBC reported. The sentence was reduced from seven years at a first trial in April. The man had joined CXMT in 2016.

CNBC said the case shows how the race for top engineering talent is increasingly at odds with efforts to protect trade secrets as Chinese chipmakers narrow the gap with established rivals. Counterpoint Research's Jeongku Choi said Chinese firms have recruited experienced overseas engineers with high salaries, stock options, housing and family support, and that their expertise has helped them overcome technical bottlenecks as U.S. export restrictions limit access to advanced equipment. Counterpoint projected CXMT's share of global DRAM revenue would reach 10% in the second quarter of 2026.

A former Samsung employee said the company once worried mainly about staff leaving for SK Hynix and Micron. Samsung monitored where departing employees went and used two-year non-compete agreements, the person said. In 2023, a South Korean court blocked a former Samsung DRAM researcher from joining Micron, ruling the non-compete was necessary to protect the company. South Korea has also designated certain chipmaking technologies as National Core Technologies, which raises penalties for leaks, according to Choi.

Lawyers quoted by CNBC described a mixed legal picture. Taiwan limits non-competes to two years and requires pay during the restricted period. Singapore and Hong Kong enforce them only when reasonable. Attorneys said proving misuse of manufacturing know-how is hard because "the trade secret is carried in the employee's head." They expect trade secret litigation to rise as competition for talent intensifies.
